content: The prevention and control of dengue require a multifaceted approach, including epidemiological and entomological surveillance, vector control, and health planning. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease that has become a significant global health threat, with its incidence increasing thirtyfold over the past 50 years. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 50 to 100 million dengue infections occur annually, with nearly half the world's population living in endemic areas. The disease imposes a staggering human and economic burden, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Dengue outbreaks are increasingly explosive, causing severe societal disruptions and economic losses. The disease is now the most important mosquito-borne viral illness globally, with epidemics resulting in human suffering, strained healthcare systems, and massive economic costs. In some regions, the burden of dengue is comparable to that of tuberculosis and other high-burden communicable diseases. For example, in 2008, an outbreak in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, resulted in over 158,000 reported cases, 9,000 hospital admissions, and 230 deaths within a few months, necessitating military intervention to support healthcare and vector control efforts. The emergence and spread of all four dengue virus serotypes across Asia, the Americas, Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean regions represent a global pandemic threat. Despite the alarming trends, there has been little globally coordinated action against dengue. The 1995 WHO strategy for dengue control is outdated and requires revision in light of new advances in vector control, diagnostics, and vaccine development. The WHO's Global Strategy for Dengue Prevention and Control (2012–2020) aims to reduce the burden of dengue by decreasing mortality by at least 50% and morbidity by 25% by 2020, using 2010 as the baseline. This strategy emphasizes proactive risk assessment, early warning systems, and preventive measures guided by entomological and epidemiological surveillance. It also highlights the importance of integrating prevention, surveillance, and case management into existing health systems to ensure efforts are coherent, sustainable, cost-effective, and ecologically sound. Reducing dengue mortality requires early case detection, appropriate management of severe cases, and reorientation of health services to effectively manage outbreaks. Training healthcare personnel and establishing robust referral systems at primary healthcare levels are critical. Morbidity can be reduced through improved outbreak prediction and detection, integrated vector management, and locally adapted vector control measures, such as effective urban and household water management. Communication strategies are essential to achieve behavioral changes that enhance prevention programs. Research plays a vital role in reversing the trend of dengue by improving surveillance, prevention, and control methods. Accurate estimates of the disease burden are necessary to assess the progress of prevention measures. Enhanced surveillance systems and dedicated studies require additional investment, particularly in endemic countries. The anticipated availability of a dengue vaccine within the next few years offers a promising opportunity to complement existing prevention and control tools. The global strategy underscores the need for coordinated action among governments, organizations, and international partners. It promotes an integrated approach to vector management and sustained control measures at all levels. National commitments to dengue control align with the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005), which obligate countries to build resilience against epidemic-prone diseases through surveillance, preparedness, and timely public health responses. In conclusion, dengue prevention and management can leverage advances in vector control technology, diagnostics, clinical interventions, and vaccine development. Effective integration of these tools into prevention and control strategies is essential to reduce the disease's burden. Increased research funding and international collaboration are critical to achieving the overarching goal of reducing dengue morbidity and mortality. With correct and timely interventions, mortality from dengue can be reduced to zero, making this a shared and achievable objective.
